Reporting regression results

Extracting model estimates and data structure

Author
Affiliation

Daniela Palleschi

Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin

Published

July 9, 2024

Learning objectives

Today we will…

  • run our first linear (mixed) model
  • produce model summary tables
  • report random effects
  • do the same with a Bayesian model

Resources

Set-up

Packages

  • we’ll need the following packages for today
pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  lme4,
  broom,
  broom.mixed,
  brms
)

Data

  • we’ll need the dataset we’ve been working with
df_lifetime <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "tidy_data_lifetime_pilot.csv"), 
                               # for special characters
                               locale = readr::locale(encoding = "latin1") 
                               ) |>
  mutate_if(is.character,as.factor) |> # all character variables as factor
  filter(type == "critical", # only critical trials
         px != "px3") # this participant had lots of 0's for some reason

Data dictionary

  • let’s review the data dictionary
dict_lifetime <- read_csv(
  here::here("data", "tidy_data_lifetime_pilot_dictionary.csv")
)

Model prep

  • we want to only have critical items
df_lifetime <-
  df_lifetime |>
  filter(type == "critical") |>
  droplevels()

  • we want our predictors (lifetime and tense) to be factors
df_lifetime$lifetime <- as.factor(df_lifetime$lifetime)
df_lifetime$tense <- as.factor(df_lifetime$tense)

  • and to have sum contrast coding:
    • PP and living are -0,5
    • SF and dead are +0,5
contrasts(df_lifetime$lifetime)
       living
dead        0
living      1
contrasts(df_lifetime$tense)
   SF
PP  0
SF  1
  • we see the default treatment (or ‘dummy’) contrasts here
  • to change them:
contrasts(df_lifetime$lifetime) <- c(-0.5, +0.5)
contrasts(df_lifetime$tense) <- c(+0.5, -0.5)
contrasts(df_lifetime$lifetime)
       [,1]
dead   -0.5
living  0.5
contrasts(df_lifetime$tense)
   [,1]
PP  0.5
SF -0.5

1 Linear regression

lm(
  log(fp) ~ tense * lifetime,
  subset = region == "verb" & ff > 0,
  data = df_lifetime
)

Call:
lm(formula = log(fp) ~ tense * lifetime, data = df_lifetime, 
    subset = region == "verb" & ff > 0)

Coefficients:
     (Intercept)            tense1         lifetime1  tense1:lifetime1  
         5.63477           0.03357          -0.10130          -0.08320

1.1 Naming conventions

  • we want to store our model as an object in the Environment
    • always try to use a prefix that defines what the object is
    • e.g., fit_, mod_, lm_, glm_
    • whatever you choose, be consistent within your project
lm_fp <-
  lm(
  log(fp) ~ tense * lifetime,
  subset = region == "verb" & ff > 0,
  data = df_lifetime
)

1.2 Model summary

  • the most straightforward way to inspect your model and the results is with summary()
summary(lm_fp)

1.3 Extracting information

  • lme4 objects contains lots of information
    • navigate to the model object in your Environment and explore the elements
  • nobs(model) will tell you how many data points were included in the model
  • formula(model) will give you the model formula
nobs(lm_fp)
[1] 543
formula(lm_fp)
log(fp) ~ tense * lifetime
  • want to check which contrasts were used in your model?
lm_fp$contrasts
$tense
   [,1]
PP  0.5
SF -0.5

$lifetime
       [,1]
dead   -0.5
living  0.5

1.4 Model reporting

  • when you run your models, you’ll want to also print the output

    • this way you avoid needing to re-run your code to see the results

  • for lme4 models we can use summary()

  • number of participants in your model

summary(lm_fp)$ngrps["px"]
NULL

2 Running models reproducibly

  • as your models get more computational complex, they can take time to fit
    • sometimes you also run several models in the same script
  • with literate programming, we want to be able to produce dynamic reports
    • we don’t want to run our models anew every time we re-render our document!
    • this also might result in different results if e.g., we update a package or R version
    • or if we send the script to somebody else with a different set-up
  • ideally, we would have our source code, output (results), and the actual model all stored and retrievable

3 Model reporting

  • when you run your models, you’ll want to also print the output
    • this way you avoid needing to re-run your code to see the results
  • for lme4 models we can use summary()

3.1 broom

  • the broom package also contains useful functions for reporting lme4 models
    • broom::tidy() produces the model estimates for our fixed effects

3.2 Publication-ready tables

  • we’ve already seen how to produce publication-ready tables
    • TASK: produce a summary of the fixed effects of a model and feed it into our knitr and kableExtra functions to produce a publication-ready table

4 Mixed models

  • the assumption of independence is often violated
    • due to multiple observations collected from e.g., the same person or item, language, etc.
  • this can lead to the inflation of Type I error (the chance of a false positive)
  • to account for this nonindependence of data points, we can used mixed models
    • mixed because they contain fixed effects (i.e., our predictors at the population-level) as well as random effects (group-level overall means and predictor effects)

4.1 lmer()

lmer_lifetime <-
  lmer(log(fp)  ~ tense * lifetime +
         (1|px) + (1|item_id),
       subset = region == "verb" & fp > 0,
       data = df_lifetime)

4.2 summary()

summary(lmer_lifetime)

4.3 broom.mixed

  • the broom.mixed package also contains useful functions for reporting lme4 mixed models
    • broom.mixed::tidy() produces the model estimates for fixed and random effects
    • if you only want fixed effects, use the argument effects = "fixed"
    • if you only want random effects, use the argument effects = "ran_pars"

4.3.1 tidy()

tidy_lmer_lifetime <- broom.mixed::tidy(lmer_lifetime)
tidy_lmer_lifetime

4.4 lmerTest

  • is something missing from our model summary?
    • which effects were statistically significant (p < .05)?
  • calculating p-values is not trivial
    • lme4 doesn’t do it for linear models
  • we can use the lmerTest package, which also has lme4
lmerTest_lifetime <-
  lmerTest::lmer(log(fp)  ~ tense * lifetime +
         (1|px) + (1|item_id),
       subset = region == "verb" & fp > 0,
       data = df_lifetime)
tidy_lmerTest_lifetime <- broom.mixed::tidy(lmerTest_lifetime)
tidy_lmerTest_lifetime
# A tibble: 7 × 8

4.4.1 Publication-ready tables

  • we’ve already seen how to produce publication-ready tables
    • TASK: produce publication-ready tables using knitr and kableExtra for:
      • a table of the model estimates of the fixed effects of our model
      • a table of the model estimates of the random effects of our model
      • a table of the with both the fixed and random effects
  • produce one of these tables as LaTeX code (if you haven’t already)
    • can you then produce this table in Overleaf?

5 How to report

  • you would typically have a (sub)section called Data Analysis which includes all the steps taken prior to inspecting your results
    • i.e., how you prepared and analysed your data
    • this should be information stated in a pre-registration but in the past tense
  • this would typically be followed by a Results section
    • containing the results from these cleaning/analysis steps

5.1 Data analysis

  • should include, e.g.,
    • model summaries in tables and/or in-text
    • any inclusion/exclusion criteria for participants or observations
    • any transformations performed on dependent or independent variables
      • e.g., we log-transformed first-pass reading times, and used sum contrast coding for our two 2-level predictors
      • we should therefore define which levels were coded as what value (+/-0.5)
  • model selection
    • what model did you start with? E.g., maximal model given the data and research questions (à la barr_random_maximal_2013?)
    • how did you handle convergence issues? E.g., parsimonious model selection (à la bates_parsimonious_2015?)

5.2 Results

  • this would be followed by a section called Results, which reports e.g.,
    • the number of participants and trials ex-/included in analyses
    • possibly raw means and 95% confidence intervals
    • model formula
    • information about the number of observations per model
  • a structure overview of model results

5.3 Example model report

An effect of *lifetime* was found in first-pass reading times at the verb region (Est = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$estimate[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="lifetime1"],2)`, *t* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$statistic[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="lifetime1"],2)`, *p* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$p.value[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="lifetime1"],2)`). A significant effect of *tense* was not found found (Est = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$estimate[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1"],2)`, *t* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$statistic[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1"],2)`, *p* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$p.value[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1"],2)`), nor an interaction of *lifetime* and *tense* (Est = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$estimate[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1:lifetime1"],2)`, *t* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$statistic[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1:lifetime1"],2)`, *p* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$p.value[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1:lifetime1"],2)`).

5.4 Output

An effect of lifetime was found in first-pass reading times at the verb region (Est = -0.1, t = -3, p = 0.0025). A significant effect of tense was not found found (Est = 0.038, t = 1.1, p = 0.26), nor an interaction of lifetime and tense (Est = -0.096, t = -1.4, p = 0.16).

6 Bayesian models

  • this is an incredibly quick introduction to Bayesian linear regression
    • there is a lot of information that I’m glossing over
  • the point here is to expose you to (potentially) your first Bayesian model
    • and to see how similar the input and output is to frequentist models

6.1 brms

  • Stan is a language for producing Bayesian models
  • brms is an R-user-friendly package to fit Bayesian models with Stan in the background
    • the function brm() can be used to fixed mixed models
  • it doesn’t have the subset argument, so let’s first filter our data accordingly
df_lifetime_verb <-
  df_lifetime |>
  filter(region == "verb",
         fp > 0)

6.2 brm()

brm_fp <-
  brm(fp ~ tense * lifetime,
    family = lognormal(),
    data = df_lifetime_verb)

6.3 Saving our model

  • brms models have a nice argument where you can specify where to save a model directly: file =
    • this is extremely useful as your models get more complex, because Bayesian models especially can take a long time to run
brm_fp <-
  brm(fp ~ tense * lifetime,
    family = lognormal(),
    data = df_lifetime_verb,
    file = here::here("models", "brm_fp"))

6.4 Mixed models in brm()

  • we can use the same function, just specify random effects
brm_fp <-
  brm(fp ~ tense * lifetime +
        (1|item) + (1|px),
    family = lognormal(),
    data = df_lifetime_verb,
    file = here::here("models", "brm_fp"))
summary(brm_fp)
 Family: lognormal 
  Links: mu = identity; sigma = identity 
Formula: fp ~ tense * lifetime 
   Data: df_lifetime_verb (Number of observations: 543) 
  Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1;
         total post-warmup draws = 4000

Regression Coefficients:
                 Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
Intercept            5.63      0.02     5.60     5.67 1.00     4507     3386
tense1               0.03      0.04    -0.04     0.11 1.00     5252     3241
lifetime1           -0.10      0.04    -0.17    -0.03 1.00     4313     3173
tense1:lifetime1    -0.08      0.07    -0.23     0.07 1.00     5040     3227

Further Distributional Parameters:
      Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS
sigma     0.44      0.01     0.41     0.47 1.00     5471     3106

Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS
and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential
scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1).
  • the output is the same…why’s that?
    • when we specify file =, brms will first look to see if such a file already exists
    • if it does, it simply loads in that model rather than fitting the model
    • the downside is that it doesn’t check if the model formula has changed, so we might not be fitting the model at all!
  • to work around this, either
    • delete the file with the same name, if you’re sure you want to overwrite it
    • change the filename (which I suggest always matches the object name in your script)
  • we’ll do the latter
brm_fp_mixed <-
  brm(fp ~ tense * lifetime +
        (1|item_id) + (1|px),
    family = lognormal(),
    data = df_lifetime_verb,
    file = here::here("models", "brm_fp_mixed"))
summary(brm_fp_mixed)

7 Plotting our brms model

plot(brm_fp_mixed)
pp_check(brm_fp_mixed)
  • the thick dark line is the posterior distribution
    • i.e., what our model fit based on the data
  • the thin blue lines represent 10 random draws/distributions from the model

9 Citing resources

  • you should cite the packages you used to fit your models
    • as well as other package versions used (but SessionInfo() also takes care of this)
  • to cite packages in-text, you can first extract the citation: with
citation(package = "brms")
To cite brms in publications use:

  Paul-Christian Bürkner (2017). brms: An R Package for Bayesian
  Multilevel Models Using Stan. Journal of Statistical Software, 80(1),
  1-28. doi:10.18637/jss.v080.i01

Paul-Christian Bürkner (2018). Advanced Bayesian Multilevel Modeling
with the R Package brms. The R Journal, 10(1), 395-411.
doi:10.32614/RJ-2018-017

Paul-Christian Bürkner (2021). Bayesian Item Response Modeling in R
with brms and Stan. Journal of Statistical Software, 100(5), 1-54.
doi:10.18637/jss.v100.i05

To see these entries in BibTeX format, use 'print(<citation>,
bibtex=TRUE)', 'toBibtex(.)', or set
'options(citation.bibtex.max=999)'.
  • or as BibTeX citation:
print(citation(package = "brms"), bibtex=TRUE)
To cite brms in publications use:

  Paul-Christian Bürkner (2017). brms: An R Package for Bayesian
  Multilevel Models Using Stan. Journal of Statistical Software, 80(1),
  1-28. doi:10.18637/jss.v080.i01

A BibTeX entry for LaTeX users is

  @Article{,
    title = {{brms}: An {R} Package for {Bayesian} Multilevel Models Using {Stan}},
    author = {Paul-Christian Bürkner},
    journal = {Journal of Statistical Software},
    year = {2017},
    volume = {80},
    number = {1},
    pages = {1--28},
    doi = {10.18637/jss.v080.i01},
    encoding = {UTF-8},
  }

Paul-Christian Bürkner (2018). Advanced Bayesian Multilevel Modeling
with the R Package brms. The R Journal, 10(1), 395-411.
doi:10.32614/RJ-2018-017

A BibTeX entry for LaTeX users is

  @Article{,
    title = {Advanced {Bayesian} Multilevel Modeling with the {R} Package {brms}},
    author = {Paul-Christian Bürkner},
    journal = {The R Journal},
    year = {2018},
    volume = {10},
    number = {1},
    pages = {395--411},
    doi = {10.32614/RJ-2018-017},
    encoding = {UTF-8},
  }

Paul-Christian Bürkner (2021). Bayesian Item Response Modeling in R
with brms and Stan. Journal of Statistical Software, 100(5), 1-54.
doi:10.18637/jss.v100.i05

A BibTeX entry for LaTeX users is

  @Article{,
    title = {Bayesian Item Response Modeling in {R} with {brms} and {Stan}},
    author = {Paul-Christian Bürkner},
    journal = {Journal of Statistical Software},
    year = {2021},
    volume = {100},
    number = {5},
    pages = {1--54},
    doi = {10.18637/jss.v100.i05},
    encoding = {UTF-8},
  }
  • then copy it to your .bib file, add a citation reference key (e.g., burkner_bayesian_2021), and cite it in-text with @burkner_bayesian_2021, which will be formatted as Bürkner (2021)
    • alternatively, save the package reference in Zotero and access it using rbbt
    • e.g., copy the DOI then find the Zotero button for ‘Add Item by Identifier’

# Learning objectives {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Today we will...

- run our first linear (mixed) model
- produce model summary tables
- report random effects
- do the same with a Bayesian model

# Resources {.unnumbered .unlisted}

# Set-up {-}

## Packages {-}

- we'll need the following packages for today

```{r}
pacman::p_load(
  tidyverse,
  lme4,
  broom,
  broom.mixed,
  brms
)
```


## Data {-}

- we'll need the dataset we've been working with

```{r}
df_lifetime <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "tidy_data_lifetime_pilot.csv"), 
                               # for special characters
                               locale = readr::locale(encoding = "latin1") 
                               ) |>
  mutate_if(is.character,as.factor) |> # all character variables as factor
  filter(type == "critical", # only critical trials
         px != "px3") # this participant had lots of 0's for some reason
```

## Data dictionary {-}

- let's review the data dictionary

```{r}
dict_lifetime <- read_csv(
  here::here("data", "tidy_data_lifetime_pilot_dictionary.csv")
)
```

## Model prep {-}

- we want to only have critical items

```{r}
df_lifetime <-
  df_lifetime |>
  filter(type == "critical") |>
  droplevels()
```

## {-}

- we want our predictors (`lifetime` and `tense`) to be factors

```{r}
df_lifetime$lifetime <- as.factor(df_lifetime$lifetime)
df_lifetime$tense <- as.factor(df_lifetime$tense)
```

## {-}

- and to have sum contrast coding:
  + `PP` and `living` are `-0,5`
  + `SF` and `dead` are `+0,5`

```{r}
contrasts(df_lifetime$lifetime)
contrasts(df_lifetime$tense)
```

- we see the default treatment (or 'dummy') contrasts here
- to change them:

```{r}
contrasts(df_lifetime$lifetime) <- c(-0.5, +0.5)
contrasts(df_lifetime$tense) <- c(+0.5, -0.5)
```

```{r}
contrasts(df_lifetime$lifetime)
contrasts(df_lifetime$tense)
```

# Linear regression

-

```{r}
lm(
  log(fp) ~ tense * lifetime,
  subset = region == "verb" & ff > 0,
  data = df_lifetime
)
```

## Naming conventions

- we want to store our model as an object in the Environment
  + always try to use a prefix that defines what the object is
  + e.g., `fit_`, `mod_`, `lm_`, `glm_`
  + whatever you choose, be consistent within your project

```{r}
lm_fp <-
  lm(
  log(fp) ~ tense * lifetime,
  subset = region == "verb" & ff > 0,
  data = df_lifetime
)
```

## Model summary

- the most straightforward way to inspect your model and the results is with `summary()`

```{r}
#| output-location: slide
summary(lm_fp)
```

## Extracting information

- `lme4` objects contains lots of information
  + navigate to the model object in your Environment and explore the elements

- `nobs(model)` will tell you how many data points were included in the model
- `formula(model)` will give you the model formula

```{r}
nobs(lm_fp)
formula(lm_fp)
```

- want to check which contrasts were used in your model?

```{r}
lm_fp$contrasts
```

## Model reporting

- when you run your models, you'll want to also print the output
  + this way you avoid needing to re-run your code to see the results
- for `lme4` models we can use `summary()`

- number of participants in your model

```{r}
summary(lm_fp)$ngrps["px"]
```

# Running models reproducibly

- as your models get more computational complex, they can take time to fit
  + sometimes you also run several models in the same script
- with literate programming, we want to be able to produce dynamic reports
  + we don't want to run our models anew every time we re-render our document!
  + this also might result in different results if e.g., we update a package or R version
  + or if we send the script to somebody else with a different set-up
- ideally, we would have our source code, output (results), *and* the actual model all stored and retrievable

# Model reporting

- when you run your models, you'll want to also print the output
  + this way you avoid needing to re-run your code to see the results
- for `lme4` models we can use `summary()`

## `broom`

- the `broom` package also contains useful functions for reporting `lme4` models
  + `broom::tidy()` produces the model estimates for our fixed effects

## Publication-ready tables

- we've already seen how to produce publication-ready tables
  + TASK: produce a summary of the fixed effects of a model and feed it into our `knitr` and `kableExtra` functions to produce a publication-ready table

# Mixed models

- the assumption of independence is often violated
  + due to multiple observations collected from e.g., the same person or item, language, etc.
- this can lead to the inflation of Type I error (the chance of a false positive)
- to account for this nonindependence of data points, we can used *mixed* models
  + *mixed* because they contain fixed effects (i.e., our predictors at the population-level) as well as *random* effects (group-level overall means and predictor effects)
  
## `lmer()`

```{r}
lmer_lifetime <-
  lmer(log(fp)  ~ tense * lifetime +
         (1|px) + (1|item_id),
       subset = region == "verb" & fp > 0,
       data = df_lifetime)
```

## `summary()`

```{r}
summary(lmer_lifetime)
```

## `broom.mixed`

- the `broom.mixed` package also contains useful functions for reporting `lme4` mixed models
  + `broom.mixed::tidy()` produces the model estimates for fixed and random effects
  + if you only want fixed effects, use the argument `effects = "fixed"`
  + if you only want random effects, use the argument `effects = "ran_pars"`
  
### `tidy()`

```{r}
tidy_lmer_lifetime <- broom.mixed::tidy(lmer_lifetime)
```

```{r}
tidy_lmer_lifetime
```

## `lmerTest`

- is something missing from our model summary?
  + which effects were statistically significant (*p* < .05)?
- calculating *p*-values is not trivial
  + `lme4` doesn't do it for linear models
- we can use the `lmerTest` package, which also has `lme4`

```{r}
lmerTest_lifetime <-
  lmerTest::lmer(log(fp)  ~ tense * lifetime +
         (1|px) + (1|item_id),
       subset = region == "verb" & fp > 0,
       data = df_lifetime)
```

```{r}
tidy_lmerTest_lifetime <- broom.mixed::tidy(lmerTest_lifetime)
```

```{r}
tidy_lmerTest_lifetime
```

### Publication-ready tables

- we've already seen how to produce publication-ready tables
  + TASK: produce publication-ready tables using `knitr` and `kableExtra` for:
    + a table of the model estimates of the fixed effects of our model
    + a table of the model estimates of the random effects of our model
    + a table of the with both the fixed and random effects
- produce one of these tables as LaTeX code (if you haven't already)
  + can you then produce this table in Overleaf?


# How to report

- you would typically have a (sub)section called Data Analysis which includes all the steps taken prior to inspecting your results
  + i.e., how you prepared and analysed your data
  + this should be information stated in a pre-registration but in the past tense
- this would typically be followed by a Results section
  + containing the results from these cleaning/analysis steps


## Data analysis

- should include, e.g.,
  + model summaries in tables and/or in-text
  - any inclusion/exclusion criteria for participants or observations
  + any transformations performed on dependent or independent variables
    + e.g., we log-transformed first-pass reading times, and used sum contrast coding for our two 2-level predictors
    + we should therefore define which levels were coded as what value (+/-0.5)
- model selection
  + what model did you start with? E.g., maximal model given the data and research questions [à la @barr_random_maximal_2013]
  + how did you handle convergence issues? E.g., parsimonious model selection [à la @bates_parsimonious_2015]

## Results

- this would be followed by a section called Results, which reports e.g.,
  + the number of participants and trials ex-/included in analyses
  + possibly raw means and 95% confidence intervals
  + model formula
  + information about the number of observations per model
- a structure overview of model results

## Example model report

```{markdown}
An effect of *lifetime* was found in first-pass reading times at the verb region (Est = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$estimate[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="lifetime1"],2)`, *t* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$statistic[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="lifetime1"],2)`, *p* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$p.value[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="lifetime1"],2)`). A significant effect of *tense* was not found found (Est = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$estimate[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1"],2)`, *t* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$statistic[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1"],2)`, *p* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$p.value[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1"],2)`), nor an interaction of *lifetime* and *tense* (Est = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$estimate[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1:lifetime1"],2)`, *t* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$statistic[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1:lifetime1"],2)`, *p* = `r signif(tidy_lmerTest_lifetime$p.value[tidy_lmer_lifetime$term=="tense1:lifetime1"],2)`).
```

# Bayesian models

- this is an incredibly quick introduction to Bayesian linear regression
  + there is a lot of information that I'm glossing over
- the point here is to expose you to (potentially) your first Bayesian model
  + and to see how similar the input and output is to frequentist models

## `brms`

- `Stan` is a language for producing Bayesian models
- `brms` is an R-user-friendly package to fit Bayesian models with `Stan` in the background
  + the function `brm()` can be used to fixed mixed models
- it doesn't have the `subset` argument, so let's first filter our data accordingly

```{r}
df_lifetime_verb <-
  df_lifetime |>
  filter(region == "verb",
         fp > 0)
```

## `brm()`

```{r}
#| eval: false
brm_fp <-
  brm(fp ~ tense * lifetime,
    family = lognormal(),
    data = df_lifetime_verb)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
brm_fp <-
  brm(fp ~ tense * lifetime,
    family = lognormal(),
    data = df_lifetime_verb,
    file = here::here("models", "brm_fp"))
```


## Saving our model

- `brms` models have a nice argument where you can specify where to save a model directly: `file =`
  + this is extremely useful as your models get more complex, because Bayesian models especially can take a long time to run

```{r}
brm_fp <-
  brm(fp ~ tense * lifetime,
    family = lognormal(),
    data = df_lifetime_verb,
    file = here::here("models", "brm_fp"))
```

## Mixed models in `brm()`

- we can use the same function, just specify random effects

```{r}
brm_fp <-
  brm(fp ~ tense * lifetime +
        (1|item) + (1|px),
    family = lognormal(),
    data = df_lifetime_verb,
    file = here::here("models", "brm_fp"))
```

```{r}
summary(brm_fp)
```

- the output is the same...why's that?
  + when we specify `file =`, `brms` will first look to see if such a file already exists
  + if it does, it simply loads in that model rather than fitting the model
  + the downside is that it doesn't check if the model formula has changed, so we might not be fitting the model at all!
- to work around this, either
  + delete the file with the same name, if you're *sure* you want to overwrite it
  + change the filename (which I suggest always matches the object name in your script)
- we'll do the latter

```{r}
brm_fp_mixed <-
  brm(fp ~ tense * lifetime +
        (1|item_id) + (1|px),
    family = lognormal(),
    data = df_lifetime_verb,
    file = here::here("models", "brm_fp_mixed"))
```

```{r}
summary(brm_fp_mixed)
```

# Plotting our brms model

```{r}
plot(brm_fp_mixed)
```

```{r}
pp_check(brm_fp_mixed)
```

- the thick dark line is the *posterior distribution*
  + i.e., what our model fit based on the data
- the thin blue lines represent 10 random draws/distributions from the model

# Citing resources

- you should cite the packages you used to fit your models
  + as well as other package versions used (but `SessionInfo()` also takes care of this)
- to cite packages in-text, you can first extract the citation: with

```{r}
citation(package = "brms")
```

- or as BibTeX citation:

```{r}
print(citation(package = "brms"), bibtex=TRUE)
```

- then copy it to your `.bib` file, add a citation reference key (e.g., `burkner_bayesian_2021`), and cite it in-text with `@burkner_bayesian_2021`, which will be formatted as @burkner_bayesian_2021
  + alternatively, save the package reference in Zotero and access it using `rbbt`
  + e.g., copy the DOI then find the Zotero button for 'Add Item by Identifier'
